newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bestsellers publishing lifeblood, says top U.S exec.
newsitem.headline: Bestsellers publishing lifeblood, says top U.S exec.

text.p: Bestsellers are the lifeblood of the book business especially when times are tough in the industry, a leading U.S. publisher said on Friday.

Comforted and cushioned by the mammoth sales of John Grisham and Danielle Steel, Bantam Doubleday Dell chairman Jack Hoeft told Reuters at the world's biggest book fair: "The big companies have to have hits."
"The business is more and more dependent on the hits and it is harder today to make a bestseller,"' he said at the fair which has attracted 9,200 publishers from 110 countries.

Echoing the pessimism of Random House chairman Alberto Vitaly about prospects for the U.S. publishing industry, Hoeft said: "It is a difficult market and I see things difficult for the next 12 to 18 months."
Like every publisher hunting for the elusive unknown who has written an international blockbuster, he said: "If I knew what the formula is, I would sell it."
Grisham certainly seems to have found that formula with his taut legal thrillers like "The Client" and "The Firm" which Hollywood has also turned into box office hits.
"Stores open at midnight on sales day when one of his comes out. We have never had that with books before," Hoeft said.
Literary agents like Andrew Wylie, known in the trade as "The Jackal," have won huge advances for their authors and revel in hype when trying to tempt publishers to loosen their purse strings.
Hoeft said of the phenomenon: "Good literary agents are important. They help in a good publishing relationship. But there are bad as well as good."
Inevitably agents pander to the insecurities of publishers fearful of missing out on a great deal.

"The agent is there to hype a book. The fools are the publishers who respond. Why be afraid of the word No," said Patrick Janson-Smith of Transworld Publishers which have Frederick Forsyth and now Gerald Seymour in their stable.
"The threat is always that if you leave the deal until Frankfurt, everyone will know about it and there will be a fever to acquire the book," he said.
"The industry is still totally out of control. It is an industry of insecurity. Publishers are easily manipulated. This is the age of the agent," he added.
In these belt-tightening times, long gone are the days when editors would stagger back from Frankfurt having spent fortunes on rights to books that never paid back their advances.
"The days of acquiring books for crazy prices at Frankfurt have gone," said Val Hudson of HarperCollins.

"It would be nice to think we could stop the upward spiral of advances but there will always be one publisher who wants that book more than any other. Some of the headline deals are not going to make money."
